title: What Is TI-81/82/83? — Definition
body:
Calculating instruments before the microchip: the abacus, Napier's bones, the slide rule (1620s–1970s), mechanical adding machines and comptometers, the Curta, and the first electronic calculators (Anita, HP-35, TI) that killed the slide rule in a decade.

In the context of this database, the TI-81/82/83 is presented as one calculator record among the calculators and math instruments family. 1990's graphing: the 81's pixels — the classroom's 1990s.

title: Origins and History of TI-81/82/83
body:
The TI-81/82/83 belongs to the 1990–2000s era and traces to TI.

The abacus (Mesopotamia, ~2700 BCE; suanpan, soroban variants) is still the fastest by hand in trained hands. Napier's bones (1617) mechanized multiplication; William Oughtred's slide rule (c. 1622) turned logs into a pocket computer that built empires — engineers used them into the Apollo era. Pascal's Pascaline (1642) and Leibniz's stepped drum led to 19th-century arithmometers; Dorr Felt's comptometer (1887) made key-driven calculation fast. The Friden, Monroe, and Marchant electromechanicals ruled offices until Anita (1961, tube/valve) and Wang LOCI brought electronics; Busicom's 1969 order led Intel to the 4004. HP-35 (1972, $395) put scientific functions in a pocket; TI's SR-50 and cheap four-bangers finished the slide rule by ~1975.

Within that longer story, TI-81/82/83: The 1990/1993; the 83's (1996) standard. The 83 is the school's graphing.

title: How TI-81/82/83 Works
body:
The abacus moves beads on rods in place-value columns — addition by bead arithmetic, multiplication by repeated shifts. The slide rule adds logarithms: align scales and read products as sums of logs (log a + log b = log ab). Mechanical calculators use stepped drums or pinwheels: cranking adds the set digits to an accumulator with carry propagation. Electronic calculators scan a key matrix, compute in BCD or binary on a chip, and drive LED/LCD displays. RPN (HP) uses a stack: enter, enter, operate — no equals key, no parentheses.

Applied to the TI-81/82/83 (1990–2000s, TI): The 83 is the school's graphing.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of TI-81/82/83 — Components
body:
Every TI-81/82/83 is an assembly of the calculators and math instruments family's standard parts:

• Beads / rods — Abacus place-value columns; heaven/earth beads.
• Logarithmic scales — C/D for multiply, A/B for squares, K for cubes, L for logs.
• Cursor / hairline — The sliding reader aligning scales.
• Stepped drum / pinwheel — Mechanical digit wheels of Leibniz/Odhner.
• Accumulator — Register holding the running total with carry.
• Keyboard — Full (comptometer) or ten-key adding layout.
• Motor / crank — Power for electromechanical calculation.
• Display — Nixie, LED, VFD, or LCD digits.
• Chip — Calculator-on-a-chip (4004 lineage).
• Solar / battery — Power; solar cells freed the pocket calc.

When examining a surviving TI-81/82/83, identify these parts in order: Beads / rods, Logarithmic scales, Cursor / hairline, Stepped drum / pinwheel, Accumulator, Keyboard.

title: TI-81/82/83 in Culture
body:
The slide rule hung on every engineer's belt like a sidearm; Apollo went to the Moon on Pickett N3s. Comptometer operators were keyboard athletes. The HP-35's $395 price was a moonshot for students — then TI made calculators disposable. Abacus competitions still draw crowds; soroban is taught in Japanese schools. 'Close enough for a slide rule' is engineering wisdom.

The TI-81/82/83 carries that cultural charge directly: The 83 is the school's graphing.

title: Collecting and Preserving TI-81/82/83
body:
Keuffel & Esser and Pickett rules: check cursor glass and scale wear. Curtas are blue-chip — verify serials and smooth cranking. Comptometers are heavy; oil per manual. Early LED calcs (HP-35, TI SR-50) need battery pack rebuilds; red-LED displays are unobtainium — buy working.

For the TI-81/82/83 specifically: 1990's graphing: the 81's pixels — the classroom's 1990s.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working TI-81/82/83 with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: TI-81/82/83 Restoration Guide
body:
Slide rules: clean with mild soap, never abrasives; replace cursor glass carefully. Mechanicals: flush old grease, oil sparingly, adjust carry levers per manual. Electronic: rebuild battery packs, recap power sections, clean key contacts.

Restoration order for a TI-81/82/83: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical calculator record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: TI-81/82/83 — Slide-rule simulator + RPN stack (Runnable Python)
body:
Multiplies by adding logarithms exactly like a slide rule, then evaluates the same expression on an HP-style RPN stack.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the TI-81/82/83 so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Slide rule math + RPN stack (public-domain concepts)
import math

def slide_rule_multiply(a, b):
    # C/D scales: log(a) + log(b), read antilog; ~3 significant figures
    logs = math.log10(a) + math.log10(b)
    mantissa = 10 ** (logs - math.floor(logs))
    decade = 10 ** math.floor(logs)
    result = mantissa * decade
    return round(result, 3 - len(str(int(result))) if result >= 1 else 3)

print("slide rule: 2.46 x 3.17 =", slide_rule_multiply(2.46, 3.17),
      "(true:", 2.46*3.17, ")")

# HP RPN: 2.46 ENTER 3.17 x
def rpn(tokens):
    st = []
    for t in tokens:
        if t in "+-*/":
            b, a = st.pop(), st.pop()
            st.append({"+" : a+b, "-": a-b, "*": a*b, "/": a/b}[t])
        else:
            st.append(float(t))
    return st[-1]
print("RPN 2.46 3.17 * =", rpn(["2.46", "3.17", "*"]))
print("RPN (5+3)*(7-2):", rpn(["5", "3", "+", "7", "2", "-", "*"]))
